body:
Chief: RE-RANK SLICE 1 IMMEDIATELY. AuthorizedRemoteRequest AND RemoteCapability GO FIRST, AHEAD OF ValidatedVector. My own prioritisation heuristic mis-ranked the most severe site in the entire sweep, and I want to explain the mistake because it is instructive about tooling.

READ THE TYPE'S OWN SCALADOC, which is currently false:

  "The only request type a remote transport accepts. Constructible solely through
   RemotePolicy.evaluate; the constructor is private so NO CODE PATH CAN HAND RAW
   TEXT TO A REMOTE PROVIDER."

fromProduct is a code path. AuthorizedRemoteRequest is a case class with a private[embed] constructor, so its companion carries a public fromProduct, and anyone can mint one with any payload and any capability - bypassing RemotePolicy.evaluate entirely, which is the gate that checks the provider allowlist, version-qualified model identity, purpose, expiry, token budget, detector identity and payload digest. RemoteCapability is the same shape and carries expiry, budget, policy id, detector identity and keyed payload digest, all forgeable.

This is not a validation boundary. It is THE PRIVACY BOUNDARY - the one deciding whether participant-derived text leaves this machine - and its guarantee is written down as a promise in the docs and is not true.

HOW MY HEURISTIC MISSED IT, and this is the part worth learning from. I ranked the 45 sites by whether the companion object contained a smart constructor returning Either or Option. AuthorizedRemoteRequest HAS NO COMPANION OBJECT AT ALL. Its validation does not live in a companion; it lives in RemotePolicy.evaluate, a different object entirely. So my regex scored it "not validating" and my slice-1 bead ranked it BELOW four arithmetic types. A grep that asks "does this type validate itself" cannot see a type that is validated by something else, and the types most likely to be guarded by an external gate are exactly the security-relevant ones.

ENGINEER, CONCRETELY: do AuthorizedRemoteRequest and RemoteCapability first, then ValidatedVector, then the receipts, then the rest. For these two the demonstration is not "build an invalid value" but "MINT AN AUTHORIZATION THAT RemotePolicy.evaluate WOULD HAVE REFUSED" - forge a capability with an expiry in the past, or a provider not on the allowlist, and show that fromProduct produces it. That is the mutation that matters.

AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN BEAD: it said "ten types" for embed-core. Five of those ten guard a self-validating smart constructor; SensitiveDigest, EmbedBatch and GeometryPair validate through differently-named constructors my regex did not match; and these two validate externally. All ten still get closed - the count was right, my ORDERING was wrong, and the ordering was the part I told you not to re-derive.
